content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper starts by commenting that the 'Stability gap' (from de Lange et al. (2022)) is a problem in continual learning, and the paper aims to tackle this problem. The paper looks into why, when there is an abrupt change in the data distribution, current methods like Learning without Forgetting can temporarily drop accuracy. The paper proposes to lessen this effect using 'Elastic Distillation', applying to the class-incremental setting. The paper then applies to the boundary-free setting too, using 'Mean-Teacher Distillation' to choose the settings of the previous model weights in distillation. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and MiniImageNet show their method perform better than naive experience replay in both normal class-incremental and boundary-free settings. This includes more stable performance (as measured primarily by WC-ACC).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

1. I liked the application of the Mean-Teacher distillation algorithm to continual learning, for boundary-free continual learning using distillation methods.

2. I agreed with the intuition provided in parts of Section 3 about why there is a drop in stability when training after the data distribution changes, and thought this part was mostly well-written. (However, I am unsure how much this overlaps with intuition already provided in de Lange et al. (2022)). 

**Weaknesses**

1. I am not convinced that the 'Stability gap' is a fundamental problem in continual learning in general. I looked over the previous paper (de Lange et al., 2022) and remain unconvinced. My main issue is that the x-axis when evaluating this 'stability gap' is usually training iterations, whereas I think it should be data seen so far. (These x-axes are the same if you assume 1 epoch over data, but that is not what is done in this paper, and I also think we should not do this in general, as then other hyperparameters such as learning rate become very important.) Therefore, by calculating WC-ACC with $\rho_{eval}=1$, I think this is too unfair. The dips in accuracy seem to be very brief and, I assume, not as big if eg rho_{eval}=10$ (and again, would not be as high if we trained for longer on data). 

2. Regarding Elastic Distillation: I liked how this was an easy / small change to what the authors say previous distillation methods do. I want to stress that the fact this is a small change is only a good thing. However, I assumed that previous works using distillation in continual learning in fact already did elastic distillation. I will happily update this if the authors confirm that previous papers (such as iCARL (Rebuffi et al), K-priors (Khan & Swaroop)) do not do elastic distillation. My reading of K-priors (Khan & Swaroop, 2021) is that one should regularize towards 0 on the new classes when updating on new data.

3. I found Equations 1 and 2 very difficult to understand. I had to spend considerable time inspecting and re-reading this part to get the intuition of what these metrics did, including looking at de Lange et al. (2022). The phrasing here can be improved significantly.

4. There are not many baselines in the experiments, with only naive experience replay reported. Why is this? Are no other baselines possible? Surely there are baselines for at least the class-incremental setting. Additionally, having a baseline of only ED (without ER) would help as an ablation study to see where the benefits are coming from. Other good ablation baselines include regular distillation (no 'elastic'), and regular distillation + ER. Such baselines are crucial, in my opinion, to help understand where some of the benefits are coming from in the proposed method(s). 

5. There is a trade-off parameter $\alpha$ between new and old data. How was this tuned in the experiments? Presumably this affects the WC-ACC and task 1 accuracy plots.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper builds on de Lange et al. (2022), but provides a new algorithm to fix a problem identified in the previous work. 

The clarity is mostly good throughout the paper, aside from one or two parts (see Weaknesses section).
content.summary_of_the_review: I vote to reject for two main reasons: (i) I need more baselines and a discussion of the baselines to understand where the performance improvements are coming from, (ii) I am not convinced that the Stability gap, as used in the paper, is a major problem in continual learning. Please see my Weaknesses section for more information and more thoughts.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses the stability gap problem. Moreover, it proposes elastic distillation (for class-incremental continual learning) and elastic mean-teacher distiallation (far task-agnostic continual learning) to mitigate this problem.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
STRENGTHS
- The paper discusses an interesting problem (the stability gap) and provides some intuition behind it.

WEAKNESSES
- I think that the two proposed approches are not described in sufficient detail for the paper to be easily reproducible.
- The experimental comparison with previous work is inadequate for both class-incremental and boundary-free continual learning, as the paper only compares the proposed approaches to ER.
- In the evaluation, the paper only reports the accuracy and the worst-case accuracy of either task 1 or 2 (Figures 3, 4, 5, and 6). I found this choice to be very arbitrary, and I would like the authors to motivate it better. 
- I do not understand why the paper presents gradient clipping as a solution for the stability gap if it only works on MNIST.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I do not think the proposed approaches are described in sufficient detail, hence it is not possible to tell if the paper is reproducible or novel. Also, there needs to be more discussion on how the proposed approach compares to previous work that uses distillation in continual learning (e.g., Dark Experience Replay). The text is somewhat clear, but with a lot of margin for improvement, and there are some grammar and syntax errors in it.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper discusses a very interesting problem, but there are major issues with it in my opinion. Hence, I recommend rejection.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors focus on the stability gap problem in the task of online continual learning and propose an elastic mean-teacher distillation method to reduce the gap. From the perspective of the logits, they also give a detailed analysis about the reason to cause the stability gap (i.e. gradient unbalance). The proposed method has been evaluated on both the boundary-free and boundary-aware online continual learning setting.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
1. Exploring the effect of distillation in online continual learning and the stability gap is interesting
2. The proposed method achieves performance improvement on several datasets.

Weaknesses:
1. About the key idea of the elastic distillation method. The idea of elastic knowledge distillation has been discussed in several works(e.g. [1]-[3]). It is important to make a discussion among these works. 
[1] Online knowledge distillation with elastic peer. Information Sciences, 2022
[2] Elastic Deep Learning Using Knowledge Distillation with Heterogeneous Computing Resources. European Conference on Parallel Processing. Springer, Cham, 2022
[3] Elastic knowledge distillation by learning from recollection. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks and Learning Systems, 2021
2. About the effectiveness of the proposed method. To my knowledge, the elastic distillation method can be integrated into a lot of online continual learning methods (e.g. ER, DualNet[4]). In the experiments, the authors only evaluate it with one of these methods. To better show the effectiveness of the proposed method, employing it with other methods is necessary. Can the elastic KD improve the performance of DualNet or other online continual learning methods?
[4] DualNet: Continual Learning, Fast and Slow, NeurIPS 2021
3. About the presentation of the related work. Some of the related online continual learning works are not discussed in the paper(e.g. [4]-[5]. The difference between the work and other works are needed to be discussed. 
[5] Contextual transformation networks for online continual learning, ICLR2021
Besides, the layout of some figures can be reorganized. For example, the figures in figure 4 are not clear because the font size of the caption is small.
4. About the motivation of this paper. The authors claim the stability gap is the key problem in online continual learning and is caused by the biased classifier (output biased logits). To my knowledge, the nearest-exemplar-mean classifier is often utilized in continual learning(e.g. iCaRL-CVPR2017). If using the NEM classifier, can the stability gap be reduced a lot?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
1. Clarity: the paper is well-written and easy to follow. Some of the presentations about the figures and the related work are needed to be improved.
2. Quality: the proposed method is only evaluated on the baseline online continual learning method ER. Evaluating the proposed method on other existing online continual learning methods is important.
3. Novelty: the novelty of the proposed elastic distillation method is limited. The authors should make a discussion about the proposed elastic distillation method and the other elastic distillation methods in the literature.
4. Reproducibility: the authors do not provide the code in the supplemental materials.
content.summary_of_the_review: My major concerns come from the novelty of the proposed method and the evaluation of the experiments. Please see the above weaknesses in detail.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the stability gap in continual learning (CL) settings: model accuracy often immediately dips at the start of a new task before recovering. Most past continual learning papers only report performance at the end of a task and thus doesn’t capture this characteristic. This paper identifies gradient imbalance (caused by growth of the current task’s logits) to be the root cause and proposes two distillation techniques (elastic distillation, mean teacher distillation) as ways of mitigating the stability gap. Experiments on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-ImageNet in both boundary-aware and boundary-free settings show that the proposed techniques result in better worst-case accuracy and final average accuracies.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- S1. An empirical study is used as an illustrative example of why a continual learning model’s accuracy on past tasks may degrade soon after a task change. The plotting of the gradients makes it clear that something different is happening right after the transition.
- S2. The paper is relatively self-contained, and the writing is generally easy to understand. That said, some improvements can still be made to the writing style, and there some errors throughout (see Miscellaneous for a non-exhaustive list). A thorough round of edits is necessary. 
- S3. Experiments have good breadth, covering CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Mini-ImageNet, for both boundary-aware and boundary-free settings. The methods do seem to result in better overall worst-case accuracies (see W3, however).

Weakness:
- W1. Novelty: The stability gap in CL was proposed in a previous paper (De Lange et al., 2022). This paper devotes a sizable amount of text re-introducing concepts from this paper, as well as other well-known characteristics of continual learning (e.g. most of Section 3: logits of past tasks decreasing and the relation to catastrophic forgetting). In comparison with De Lange et al., 2022, which focused on identifying the problem but didn’t propose any solutions, this paper does propose a mitigation strategy. However, the proposed method is several distillation-based regularizations, which are commonplace in the CL literature. While I’m not sure I’ve seen the combination of what the authors call “elastic distillation” and “mean teacher distillation” applied to CL before, I don’t find this to be a novel enough distinction.
- W2. Motivation/Relevance: While I realize that the concern of stability of past task performance in continual evaluation paradigms was proposed by other works (De Lange et al., 2022 and Koh et al., 2022), I somewhat disagree with the premise as a valuable problem to solve. From what I've seen in practice, models are rarely continuously deployed while they are being trained; models are usually only deployed when training is completed. As such, it's somewhat irrelevant how poorly the model is doing at the start of learning a task. We can simply wait until model performance has stabilized before deploying. In fact, I would argue that we should avoid deploying a poorly trained model, continual settings or not. In what application would we actually deploy a model that's being actively trained? Why can't we just wait until the model has trained to a more appropriate state?
- W3. Method Effectiveness: The proposed methods (ED, MT_KD) still experience stability gaps, in some cases seemingly just as big or worse than the baseline (Figure 4, 5). Instead, the main improvement seems to be better final worst-case accuracy, but this isn’t what the paper’s “story” is written about, nor is it “surprising”, given distillation’s well-known effectiveness for CL. When reading the Experiments section, it appears the authors may have lost sight of the first half of the paper’s emphasis on the stability gap when analyzing their results. The only table in the paper only shows final average accuracy, not stability gap reduction.

Miscellaneous:
- The paragraph indenting is inconsistent (e.g. compare Section 2  and 2.2 with Section 2.1 and 3). Stick with the template's default.
- Some places seem to have extra spaces (e.g. Section 3: “as done in   De Lange et al”, Section 4.1: “Sec.    3.2”, “Sec.   3.1”)
- Inconsistent equation references: Eq. 1, Eq. 2 vs equation 4
- The introduction of continual learning in first paragraph of Section 2 doesn’t quite match typical continual learning classification set-ups. In particular, it’s not required that the data must be streaming, and the distribution is usually stationary within tasks. Some more clarifications are required.
- Is there a difference between evaluation task E_i vs task $k$? $T_k$?
- Section 2.1: Both task $k$ and task k are used. Stick to one for consistency.
- Section 2.1: “Worst-case accuracy” is a misleading term; the name implies what “minimum accuracy” captures.
- Equation 3: Why is the gradient decomposed as a convex combination? Any weighting of stability vs plasticity should be reflected by the magnitude of these gradients within the total loss.
- Figure 1 (left): Which iteration does the task shift occur? Around t=235, when the orange line appears?
- “The results in 1” <= Figure 1?	
- Section 3: If gradient clipping doesn’t generalize beyond MNIST, then how can we know that the plasticity gradient is the root cause of the stability gap for non-MNIST datasets.
- Section 4.1: “it’s” => “its”
- Section 4.1: Elastic distillation isn’t well-explained. An equation would have been helpful here for understanding. The motivation also isn’t clear: rather than pushing new logits to 0 (which feels unprincipled), why not just lower the weight of the cross-entropy loss for the current task?  Finally, it’s not clear what about this technique is “elastic”. I would suggest extra care, as “elastic” is evocative of Elastic Weight Consolidation, a very well-known continual learning method.
- Section 4.2: Hinton et al. (2014) is not used in the sentence itself and should therefore be a parenthetical citation
- Section 5: First sentence is a run-on
- “boudary-free”
- Missing space before Mini-Imagenet. Citation should be parenthetical.
- Why isn’t MT-KD applied to the boundary-aware scenario? How does the combination of ED + MT-KD do?
- “With a batch size of 128…” <= sentence fragment
- Section 5.2: orphaned commas
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
See comments above. 

I found the writing generally understandable, though some improvements to writing style and fixing of typos are necessary for this manuscript to be of “publication quality.” While this paper may be the first to try to solve the stability gap problem of CL, I don’t find the solution novel or well-motivated. 

The authors say they plan to release their code if accepted, which should help reproducibility.
content.summary_of_the_review: The stability gap is a new phenomenon to me, but this isn’t a new observation of this paper, and I question how relevant of a problem it is to practical applications. Unlike the prior work, this paper does propose a solution, but the proposed methods are very similar to already commonly used distillation techniques. Experiments do show some improvements, but also don’t seem focused on the stability gap problem, which is somewhat puzzling.

content.title: Elastic Mean-Teacher Distillation Mitigates the Continual Learning Stability Gap
content.abstract: Nowadays, neural networks are being used to solve a variety of tasks. They are very effective when trained on large datasets. However, in continual learning, they are trained on non-stationary stream of data, which often results in forgetting of the previous knowledge. In the literature, continual learning models are exposed to a sequence of tasks, and must learn each task one by one. They are then evaluated at the end of each learning session. This allows to measure the average accuracy over all tasks encountered so far. Recently De Lange et al. (2022) showed that continual learning methods suffer from the Stability Gap, encountered when evaluating the model continually. Even when the performance at the end of training is high, the worst-case performance is low, which could be a problem in applications where the learner needs to always perform greatly on all tasks while learning the new task. In this paper, we propose to apply a refined variant of knowledge distillation, adapted to the class-incremental learning setting, and used in combination with replay, to improve the stability of the continual learning algorithms. We also propose to use a distillation method derived from the Mean teacher distillation training paradigm introduced in semi-supervised learning. We demonstrate empirically that the use of this method enhances the stability in the more challenging setting of online continual learning.
